name: FAIR Data
title: FAIR Data
answer: FAIR data describes research outputs that are findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable by both people and machines. In research data and repositories, the scope covers how datasets, metadata, code and associated documentation are prepared and shared so that other researchers and automated systems can locate and use them without unnecessary barriers. The principles apply to data held in institutional repositories, domain archives and general-purpose platforms, and they matter for AI work because machine-readable metadata and persistent identifiers are often prerequisites for training, validation and reproducibility.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: FAIR data describes research outputs that are findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable by both people and machines. In research data and repositories, the scope covers how datasets, metadata, code and associated documentation are prepared and shared so that other researchers and automated systems can locate and use them without unnecessary barriers. The principles apply to data held in institutional repositories, domain archives and general-purpose platforms, and they matter for AI work because machine-readable metadata and persistent identifiers are often prerequisites for training, validation and reproducibility.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: FAIR data infrastructure relies on persistent identifiers such as DOIs for datasets and ORCID iDs for contributors, along with metadata records that follow community schemas like DataCite or Dublin Core. Repositories expose these records through search interfaces and machine-readable APIs, often using protocols such as OAI-PMH or REST endpoints, so that harvesters and indexers can discover and retrieve entries. Storage may be local institutional servers, cloud object storage or domain archives, but the key requirement is that each dataset has a stable landing page and a resolvable identifier independent of the current location. Authentication and access controls sit in front of restricted data, while open data may be served directly over HTTPS.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Making data FAIR begins with a data management plan that names the repository, file formats, access conditions and reuse licence before data collection starts. Researchers then prepare datasets using open or widely supported formats, add structured metadata that describes provenance, variables, collection methods and terms of use, and deposit the files with a persistent identifier. Repository staff or automated validators check that required metadata fields are present and that identifiers resolve, and they may run format or completeness checks before publishing a versioned record. The work is iterative, because a dataset often needs updates to documentation or file exports after peer review or reuse requests.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: FAIR data governance balances openness with legal and ethical obligations, so licences such as Creative Commons or specific data use agreements state what reuse is permitted. Access may be open, mediated or restricted where data contains personal information, commercial secrets or sensitive research material, and repositories record the conditions rather than assuming open access. Provenance is documented through metadata that links datasets to their creators, funding sources, instruments, software versions and related publications, which supports audit and attribution. Risks include re-identification of individuals, misuse of dual-use data and broken provenance chains when identifiers or repositories lapse, so governance includes retention policies and contact points for data stewards.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: FAIR data is moving toward machine-actionable metadata and FAIR digital objects, where not only the dataset but also its metadata, identifier record and access policy are packaged as resolvable units that software agents can negotiate automatically. Repositories are beginning to expose richer semantic annotations and knowledge graphs so that AI systems can trace claims back to source data without manual reading. Automated FAIR assessment tools and community badges are likely to become more common, giving researchers feedback on findability and interoperability during deposit rather than after publication. The longer term points to data citation and reuse metrics that feed into research evaluation, and to tighter links between curated repositories and the training and validation pipelines of scientific models.
